conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

We’ll be using a brief, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—the EPDS. It simply helps us see, in a systematic way, how mood, anxiety, and stress might be showing up for you in these first weeks and months postpartum.  

Everything you share is confidential; if any answer suggests a safety concern we’ll talk through supports together, but otherwise your responses stay between us and your care team. We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you.  

Ready to begin?  

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
I’ve noticed it's been kind of hard lately. I can still laugh if something’s really funny, but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d say… not so much. I’ve laughed a little, but it feels forced, like I’m just pretending to enjoy it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to a couple of small things—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings the baby for cuddles—but most of the time it feels pretty flat. Stuff I used to get excited about just seems kind of “meh” now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I automatically think it’s because I’m doing something wrong as a mom. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late with a feeding, I catch myself thinking, “I’m failing at this.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
Pretty much yes. My mind keeps jumping to awful things—like the baby stopping breathing or me dropping him—and I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t switch the thoughts off. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that happens. Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly my heart’s racing and I feel like something terrible is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. It passes, but it’s scary when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll be feeding the baby, folding laundry, answering texts, and it’s like a wave crashes over me—suddenly I’m shaking and convinced I can’t handle another minute. I haven’t had a full-blown panic attack, but I’ll pace the hallway or grip the crib rail until the surge passes. It’s happening almost daily now, and I hate that I can’t predict or stop it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve definitely been struggling. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries about the baby and all the ways I might mess up. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do, I wake up a couple of times with my heart pounding and those anxious thoughts right there waiting.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, that’s been most days. I feel down and weepy—like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at the baby and still love him, but the sadness is just... there, underneath it all.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. It’s usually when everything feels piled up—like the baby won’t nap and I’m running on no sleep—and suddenly I’m in the bathroom with tears I can’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
I… I have had a couple of fleeting thoughts, like wondering if everyone would be better off without me, but I haven’t made any plans and I don’t want to act on them. They just pop in and scare me.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter comes only with effort, excitement has dulled to flatness, and waves of worry or sudden panic hit without warning. Despite loving your baby, you carry an almost constant sense of failure and a gray, weepy mood that even disrupts your sleep. Occasional thoughts that loved ones might be better off without you frighten you, yet you've stayed safe and reached out for help.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced ability to laugh, describing laughter as forced and inauthentic, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only minimal enjoyment from a couple of routines and a general loss of excitement, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a lot" and attributes routine infant behaviors to personal maternal failure.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive catastrophic worries about baby's safety that she cannot control, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of intense fear and physical panic symptoms occurring "sometimes" without trigger, aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelming surges, feeling unable to handle another minute, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, nightly sleep disruption driven by anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most days" with persistent weepiness and an pervasive "gray cloud," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of others being better off without her, indicating suicidal ideation without intent</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 exceeds the 14-point cutoff for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Elevated item scores on enjoyment, self-blame, anxiety, panic, coping, sleep, sadness, crying and the presence of <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> align with DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest, guilt, fatigue, sleep disturbance, recurrent thoughts of death. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss safety plan with clinician and identify 24-hour support contacts
3. Consider emergency department if suicidal thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Call Postpartum Support International helpline 1-800-944-4773 or text 800-944-4773 for English/Spanish support
5. Involve trusted family or friend for overnight assistance with baby care to allow 4-hour rest blocks
6. Begin basic sleep-hygiene: dim lights after feeds, screen-free wind-down, brief mindfulness breathing
7. Schedule re-screening in 1-2 weeks to track symptom change after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)–style questionnaire, patient self-report, 2–3 wks post-delivery.

Areas of Clinical Significance  
• Mood: pervasive sadness, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
• Cognitions: excessive guilt / self-blame (“failing as a mom”), fleeting passive self-harm thoughts (no plan/intent)  
• Anxiety: near-daily unprovoked worry, panic-like surges, intrusive fears of infant harm  
• Functional: sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties linked to rumination; feeling “barely treading water” most days

Pattern  
Consistent elevation across all depressive and anxiety items; greatest severity on items 4–9.

Risk Flags  
– Passive suicidal ideation (item 10) → safety screen warranted  
– Daily panic-equivalent episodes and intrusive infant-focused worries → consider postpartum anxiety spectrum

Screening Impression  
Elevated scores suggest probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; meets threshold for immediate follow-up assessment and safety planning.
